Article Title: Harvard scientists build a silicon chip that writes DNA with electricity, paving the way for cleaner gene synthesis and DNA-based data storage
Article Text:
Representative image

How the silicon chip works

From neuroscience to biotechnology

Potential applications

Challenges ahead

Silicon chips have long been the backbone of computing, but a Harvard-led research team has given them an entirely different job: writing DNA. As reported by Science Daily, a study published in Nature Electronics, Harvard researchers have unveiled a silicon chip DNA writer capable of synthesising DNA using electricity and water-based enzymes. The innovation marks a major departure from traditional phosphoramidite chemistry, which relies on hazardous organic solvents. The chip can simultaneously produce 64 different DNA sequences, each up to 39 nucleotides long, offering a cleaner and more scalable approach to DNA manufacturing.The project involved Harvard, the Broad Institute, DNA Script, and POSTECH, with funding from IARPA, Horizon Europe, and Samsung Research. Intellectual property has been filed by Harvard’s Office of Technology Development.The chip assembles DNA strands one nucleotide at a time. A temporary blocking group halts growth until removed under acidic conditions. By applying tiny electrical currents, the chip generates protons that lower pH locally, enabling DNA synthesis to continue. Each site is confined by concentric ring electrodes, allowing parallel construction of multiple sequences.This precise control makes the process safer and more efficient than conventional methods.Synthetic DNA is essential for diagnostics, genome engineering, and cancer research. Current methods require centralized facilities and involve toxic solvents. The Harvard chip’s water-based enzymatic process could enable portable DNA-writing devices, making the technology more accessible to labs and clinics worldwide.Interestingly, the chip’s design originated in neuroscience research, where it was used to record electrical activity in neurons. Researchers later repurposed its precision current injection technology to control chemical conditions for DNA synthesis, bridging the gap between brain science and biotechnology.* Portable DNA-writing devices for labs and hospitals* DNA data storage, demonstrated by encoding a 169-byte text* Synthetic biology and diagnostics with reduced environmental impactScaling the technology will require new chemistry. Current limitations stem from intermediate molecules drifting between synthesis sites during deprotection. Researchers are working on more direct acid-driven chemistry to overcome this hurdle, aiming for longer and more complex DNA sequences.
Article Summary: Harvard researchers have unveiled a silicon chip DNA writer capable of synthesising DNA using electricity and water-based enzymes. The innovation marks a major departure from traditional phosphoramidite chemistry, which relies on hazardous organic solvents. The chip can simultaneously produce 64 different DNA sequences, each up to 39 nucleotides long.

Article Title: G-Shock GravityMaster GWR-B3000 launched in India, priced from Rs 65,995
Article Text:
G-Shock GravityMaster GWR-B3000 lands in India from Rs 65,995, with a new TOUGH MVT.2 movement that realigns its own hands after a hard knock.

The new movement corrects its own hands after a hard knock

Casio has launched the G-Shock GravityMaster GWR-B3000 to India, a supersonic-themed pilot's watch that lands in three variants at Rs 65,995 for the GWR-B3000-1A, Rs 72,995 for the GWR-B3000A-2A and Rs 79,995 for the GWR-B3000B-8A. All three are on sale now through select G-Shock stores and online platforms, and all three run the brand's newly developed TOUGH MVT.2 movement, which is the real story here.The design brief was "Supersonic", and Casio has leaned into aviation cues throughout. The dial is wide and dimensional with oversized hands and indexes, finished in a new dark black treatment that plays with light and shadow to boost contrast. A micro-textured surface finish cuts down glare, and the sapphire crystal gets an anti-reflective coating for cockpit-grade legibility.TOUGH MVT.2 adds two things worth caring about. Shock detection with auto hand home position correction means a heavy impact triggers the watch to realign its hands on its own. Magnetic field detection pauses hand movement when the watch hits strong magnetic interference, then resumes once it clears.Tough Solar charging, Multiband 6 radio-controlled timekeeping and Bluetooth Smartphone Link round out the accuracy story.Housing all of this is a dual hollow case built to absorb shock, centrifugal force and vibration, using Triple G Resist. A carbon fibre-reinforced resin inner case sits inside stainless steel outer protectors, with topology engineering used to keep weight down without thinning out the structure.For pilots and frequent flyers, there's dual-dial world time, direct UTC access, Phone Finder and Flight Log functionality via the companion app. Casio has also worked bio-based resin into key components of the centre case and band, a quiet sustainability nod that doesn't change how the watch behaves on the wrist.
Article Summary: G-Shock GravityMaster GWR-B3000 lands in India from Rs 65,995. New TOUGH MVT.2 movement that realigns its own hands after a hard knock. Dual-dial world time, direct UTC access, Phone Finder and Flight Log.

Article Title: Sennheiser becomes official sound provider of Formula E
Article Text: Formula E has named Sennheiser as its Official Sound Provider in a new multi-year collaboration aimed at transforming the audio experience of electric racing. The partnership will integrate Sennheiser’s professional audio solutions and pioneering AMBEO immersive audio technology across the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship.As the first all-electric FIA World Championship, Formula E has consistently led in sport-tech innovation. With Sennheiser’s expertise, the series will explore advanced audio capture and encoding workflows to deliver more immersive broadcasts. Fans watching on any device will experience the excitement and energy of racing through natural, three-dimensional soundscapes.Formula E CTO Dan Cherowbrier said: “Innovation and technology are at the core of Formula E, and Sennheiser is the perfect partner to help us redefine the audio landscape of our championship.”Sennheiser Group CEO Andreas Sennheiser described the collaboration as an opportunity to rethink the role of sound in electric racing. “Great visuals deserve equally compelling sound, and we see real potential to define the sport’s unique acoustic character through dynamic in-car and trackside soundscapes,” he said.A key driver of the partnership is Sennheiser’s AMBEO ecosystem, which enables the capture, processing, and reproduction of natural, three-dimensional sound.This will allow viewers to feel more connected to the racing environment and their favorite teams.The collaboration will also enhance Formula E’s fan zones and VIP hospitality, ensuring that the championship remains at the cutting edge of sports entertainment. By combining innovation in audio with the thrill of electric racing, Formula E and Sennheiser aim to set a new benchmark for immersive motorsport experiences worldwide.
Article Summary: Formula E has named Sennheiser as its Official Sound Provider in a new multi- year collaboration aimed at transforming the audio experience of electric racing. The partnership will integrate Senn heiser’s professional audio solutions and pioneering AMBEO immersive audio technology across the ABB FIA Formula E World Championship.

Article Title: Meta’s 'spy glasses' face resistance in UK; banned by restaurants, pubs and theatres across the country
Article Text:
UK venues from Wetherspoons to Soho House are now telling customers to take off Meta's £359 smart glasses.

Restaurateurs say guest privacy ends where the hidden camera begins

The 'pervert glasses' nickname is doing more damage than any regulator

Meta's LED defence has not convinced anyone outside Meta

Meta paid Kylie Jenner to make camera glasses look like ordinary eyewear. Britain's hospitality trade has decided they are nothing of the sort. A report in The Guardian says a widening list of UK venues—high-end London dining rooms, private members' clubs, the country's largest pub chain and a major theatre group—are now telling customers to take off the £359 (roughly Rs 40,000) smart glasses, or at minimum stop filming with them.The bans land at an awkward moment for Meta. Sales tripled over the past year, with more than 7 million pairs sold worldwide, and the company has been steadily expanding the lineup with celebrity-fronted designs. But the same discretion that makes the glasses appealing to wear is exactly what venue owners have flagged as the problem. A phone pointed at a table is obvious. A pair of cat-eye frames is not.Jeremy King, who runs London venues including Simpsons in the Strand, Arlington and The Park, told The Guardian he would never knowingly permit "any invasion of guest privacy other than with the eyes we were born with." Soho House confirmed filming is not allowed inside its private members' clubs, and staff can be expected to ask wearers to remove the glasses. ATG Theatres, which operates the Bristol Hippodrome, the Edinburgh Playhouse and several London houses, said the same applies during performances.Wetherspoons, with roughly 800 pubs across England and Ireland, has taken a softer line that arrives at the same place. Chief executive Tim Martin said the standard rule in his pubs, and most pubs, is that customers cannot film staff or other patrons without permission—and that the glasses appear to breach that rule by enabling surreptitious surveillance.His instinct, he said, is to tell people to switch the cameras off. Notably, phones are not banned. The distinction is intent: a phone can record people covertly, while glasses are built to.The UK restrictions follow months of reputational bleeding. The glasses have been rebranded online as "pervert glasses," a term that stuck after reports of men filming women without consent for pickup-artist content. One woman told the BBC a man recorded her and then demanded payment to take the videos down. Instagram head Adam Mosseri has said the platform will remove harassment content shot on the devices.Musician Lorde attacked them from stage at Madrid's Mad Cool festival in July, telling the crowd not to buy them. Activist collective Everyone Hates Elon has plastered fake Meta ads across London bus stops, one using an optical illusion that flips Jenner's face into a skull—a nod to John Carpenter's They Live.Meta's response has stayed consistent: every pair carries a capture LED that blinks while recording, it cannot be switched off, and the camera disables itself if the light is covered or damaged. The company says people use the glasses for music, live translation and hands-free calls.Not every operator is hostile. Michelin-starred chef Tom Kerridge told The Guardian he has no issue with them, arguing filming is simply part of modern life and can be used creatively.The bans matter beyond Meta. Courtrooms in New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin have already prohibited the devices, and Bloomberg reports Apple is delaying its own glasses partly to rework its privacy pitch before a WWDC 2027 unveiling. The category's biggest obstacle is no longer battery life. It is being allowed indoors.
Article Summary: UK venues from Wetherspoons to Soho House are now telling customers to take off Meta's £359 smart glasses. The glasses have been rebranded online as "pervert glasses," a term that stuck after reports of men filming women without consent for pickup artist content.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Italian lights to drape Futala Musical Fountain in tricolor on I-Day
Article Text:
250 high-performance LED lights imported from Italy being installed at Futala Lake in Nagpur

Nagpur:





Futala Musical Fountain will glow in the colours of the tricolour this Independence Day as 250 high-performance LED lights imported from Italy are switched on alongside a specially curated ‘Patriotic Medley’ in the evening on August 15.The exercise, being undertaken while restoration of the long-defunct fountain continues, will offer a glimpse of the sophisticated light-and-sound infrastructure being installed at the site. It will, however, not be a public show. The viewing gallery will remain closed as restoration work is still underway.Cinematographer and Futala project technical director Alphonse Roy said the ‘Patriotic Medley’ will feature a curated selection of patriotic songs, with the lighting programmed around the colours of the national flag. “It will be a purely light-and-sound presentation, as the pumps are expected to arrive after August 15. We have put together a medley of Bollywood patriotic songs, including ‘Jai Ho’ and others,” he said.Achieving colour accuracy itself requires specialised technology. The fountain has been equipped with 250 custom RGBA — red, green, blue and amber — LED fixtures imported from Italy. Unlike conventional RGB lights, the additional amber channel broadens the colour spectrum and allows warmer shades to be reproduced more naturally.“The amber channel is particularly important for getting the saffron right. It also helps us achieve cleaner whites without unwanted cool or greenish shifts,” Roy explained. The system will be programmed to reproduce saffron, white, green and navy blue during the presentation.Roy, an Emmy Award-winning cinematographer, has been closely involved in ensuring colour fidelity across the fountain’s visual programming. “Light is not just about brightness. The exact shade and how it appears against water makes a huge difference to the visual experience,” he said.The audio accompanying the display has received similar attention. Futala has been equipped with an outdoor sound system from German manufacturer d&b audiotechnik, designed to deliver high-fidelity audio across the expansive lakefront while controlling how far sound travels beyond the intended audience area.“Unlike indoor venues, outdoor spaces have no walls or ceilings to contain sound, making factors such as wind, atmospheric absorption, temperature changes and noise limits critical. The key is to direct sound precisely towards the audience while minimising spill into surrounding areas,” Roy said.The Independence Day exercise coincides with another important phase of restoration. The Belgian expert is scheduled to arrive in Nagpur on August 15 and remain stationed until August 27 to undertake specialised works. Consignments of pump components sourced from France are also expected to arrive this month as installation and integration of the fountain’s remaining systems continue.While Futala will light up in national colours on Friday, the spectacle will provide a brief glimpse of the attraction taking shape ahead of its eventual return.
Article Summary: 250 high-performance LED lights imported from Italy are switched on alongside a specially curated ‘Patriotic Medley’ in the evening on August 15. The exercise, being undertaken while restoration of the long-defunct fountain continues, will offer a glimpse of the sophisticated light-and-sound infrastructure being installed at the site.

Article Title: Mobile lab brings chemistry experiments to schoolchildren
Article Text:
Nagpur:





Chemistry enthusiast Sagar is taking his mobile laboratory to schools to make science engaging and accessible for young learners.An applied physics student with a keen interest in chemical sciences, Sagar has spent nearly a decade collecting, purifying, and studying elements. His journey began at age 21 as a hobby of collecting everyday chemical compounds. What started as a personal interest grew into a serious scientific pursuit as he studied the composition of different substances and explored ways to preserve elements in their purest forms.Over the years, Sagar built a collection of 40 distinct chemical elements in purified forms. Now, he aims to share this experience with school students through a mobile laboratory. The initiative allows students to witness live demonstrations and perform basic experiments, moving them beyond textbook learning to practical experience.Sagar believes early exposure to hands-on experiments fosters curiosity and deepens scientific understanding. He aims to make chemistry less theoretical by encouraging students to explore through observation and experimentation.Additionally, Sagar is developing tactile and sensory-based learning methods for students with visual impairments so they can experience chemistry through hands-on activities. He hopes to expand the project to more schools, encouraging young minds to view science as something to explore beyond the classroom.
Article Summary: Chemistry enthusiast Sagar is taking his mobile laboratory to schools to make science engaging and accessible for young learners. Sagar has spent nearly a decade collecting, purifying, and studying elements. He hopes to expand the project to more schools, encouraging young minds to view science as something to explore beyond the classroom.

Article Title: TSMC and Taiwan researchers engineered an interface only 0.42 nanometers thick to improve next-generation MoS2 transistors
Article Text:
Representational AI photo

Focus on Atomic Boundary

Why interface matters

Science Daily photo

0.42-nanometre buffer layer

Relevance for future chips

Researchers from Taiwan's National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University (NYCU) and TSMC Corporate Research have developed a new way to improve transistors made from atomically thin materials. They focuses on the tiny boundary where two materials meet, which allowed them to build transistors with an extremely thin insulating layer while maintaining strong electrical performance.According to Science Daily, atomically thin semiconductors have been studied for more than a decade because some can be just one atom thick while still showing useful electrical properties. Such materials could allow transistors to become smaller, faster and more energy efficient than conventional silicon-based devices.However, making these very thin transistors work well has been difficult. One major problem involves the gate dielectric, an extremely thin insulating layer that helps control the movement of electrons. Making it thinner can improve transistor control, but when it is placed on an atomically thin semiconductor, problems can develop at the boundary between the two materials. These can interfere with electron movement and reduce performance.The new study, published in Nature Electronics, addresses this problem by engineering the atomic interface between the semiconductor and the insulating layer.The NYCU team worked with TSMC Corporate Research to engineer the narrow region where the two materials meet. Instead of focusing only on finding a new semiconductor, the researchers changed the interface itself.The team used monolayer molybdenum disulfide, or MoS2, as the semiconductor. A monolayer is a material that is only one layer of atoms thick. The researchers first placed an ultrathin epitaxial aluminium layer directly on the MoS2.They then oxidised the aluminium to create an aluminium oxide layer about 0.42 nanometres thick. After this, they added a high-κ hafnium oxide gate dielectric, an insulating material that can provide strong electrical control while remaining very thin.The 0.42-nanometre aluminium oxide layer acted as a buffer between the MoS2 and hafnium oxide. It created a smoother surface, helping the hafnium oxide grow more uniformly, while also reducing unwanted electrical interactions between the two materials."For many years, efforts to improve atomically thin transistors have largely focused on discovering better semiconductor materials," said Professor Wen-Hao Chang, the study's corresponding author from NYCU. "Our research shows that the atomic interface between materials can be just as important. By engineering that boundary, we were able to reduce one of the fundamental trade-offs that has limited two-dimensional transistors for many years," he added.Atomically thin semiconductors create a particular challenge because their surfaces do not have dangling bonds. This makes it difficult to grow an extremely thin dielectric layer evenly across the surface.Standard deposition methods can leave gaps and defects at the interface. These can create electrical disorder and reduce carrier mobility, which refers to how easily electrons move through a material.Researchers have explored different dielectric materials, molecular seed layers and other oxide deposition methods. However, achieving a very thin equivalent oxide thickness, strong electrostatic control and high carrier mobility at the same time remains difficult.The challenge is especially important for wafer-scale CVD-grown monolayer MoS2. CVD, or chemical vapour deposition, is a method used to produce thin material layers over a larger area.The researchers' approach was to redesign the interface rather than replace the semiconductor or gate dielectric. They placed the ultrathin epitaxial aluminium layer on monolayer MoS2 and oxidised it to produce the 0.42-nanometre aluminium oxide layer. The high-κ hafnium oxide was then added on top.The team built short-channel top-gate transistors using CVD-grown monolayer MoS2. The devices had an equivalent oxide thickness of about one nanometre.Tests showed low leakage current and minimal hysteresis. Hysteresis refers to unwanted differences in a transistor's electrical response depending on its previous operating condition.The transistors reached a maximum transconductance of 0.45 mS μm-1, with channel lengths of about 100 nanometres. Transconductance measures how strongly a transistor's current responds when the gate voltage changes.The devices combined a very thin dielectric with strong electrical control and continued carrier transport, a combination that has been difficult to achieve in atomically thin transistors.The findings highlight the growing importance of interfaces as transistor components become smaller. When materials are only a few atomic layers thick, the region where two materials meet can strongly affect how the device performs."When transistor components become only a few atomic layers thick, the interface is no longer simply the boundary between materials, it becomes an active part of the device," said Professor Tsung-En Lee, the study's corresponding author. "Learning to engineer these interfaces with atomic precision opens new opportunities for designing future semiconductor devices that would be difficult to achieve by changing individual materials alone," professor Lee added.The researchers believe the approach could contribute to future two-dimensional electronics. Using CVD-grown monolayer MoS2 also brings the work closer to materials and processes that could eventually be considered for wafer-scale manufacturing.
Article Summary: Researchers from Taiwan's National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University have developed a new way to improve transistors made from atomically thin materials. They focuses on the tiny boundary where two materials meet, which allowed them to build transistors with an extremely thin insulating layer.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Arthur Schopenhauer: 'Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see' and the philosophy behind revolutionary thinking
Article Text:
Arthur Schopenhauer

“Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see,”

A lonely philosopher’s view of human ability

The World as Will and Representation

Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung

The philosophy of seeing beyond the self

Knowing the difference between optimization and real innovation

For known problems, use talent. Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively.

Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively. For problems caused by stagnation, make room for genius. Question basic assumptions, step away from immediate measurements and ask what possibilities are being ignored simply because they do not fit current systems.

An archer steps up to the line, pulls back the bowstring and releases an arrow that hits a bullseye two hundred yards away through thick fog. The crowd applauds the incredible skill needed to make a shot that almost nobody else could manage.Then another marksman steps forward, turns forty-five degrees away from the target range and fires an arrow into an empty part of the forest. Moments later, a target that nobody knew was hanging there falls from a high branch.wrote the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer.The difference challenges the common idea that talent and genius are simply different levels of the same ability. Talent is a quantitative advantage. It means being extremely good at working within existing rules, tools and systems. Genius is different. It is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize.Arthur Schopenhauer published this metaphor in the expanded 1844 edition of), in Chapter 31, titled “On Genius.”In the original German, Schopenhauer wrote: “Das Talent gleicht dem Schützen, der ein Ziel trifft, welches die Uebrigen nicht erreichen können; das Genie dem, der eines trifft, bis zu welchem sie nicht ein Mal zu sehn vermögen.”When Schopenhauer wrote these words in 1844, he was a bitter and largely ignored academic living in Frankfurt. The first edition of his major work, published in late 1818, had been a commercial failure. Many copies were eventually sold as wastepaper. For years, he watched contemporaries such as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel receive fame, university positions and public admiration, while Schopenhauer’s own university lectures attracted very few students.Schopenhauer believed that talent usually belongs to its own time. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Because their abilities fit existing needs, they can receive recognition, money and praise quickly.Genius works differently. Schopenhauer compared it to something like a comet entering an orderly planetary system. Because a genius works toward a goal that other people cannot yet understand, their ideas may be met with silence, confusion or even hostility during their lifetime.To understand this difference, we need to look at Schopenhauer’s larger theory of consciousness. He argued that ordinary human thinking is controlled by what he called the “Will”—a blind and constant drive toward survival, self-interest and reproduction.Talent usually works in service of this Will. A talented person uses a powerful intellect to solve practical problems, win competitions or master an existing craft. Their mind may be extremely sharp, but it remains connected to personal goals and the demands of society.Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands. Schopenhauer described genius as the ability to enter a state of “pure contemplation.” In this state, a person becomes deeply objective and temporarily forgets their ego, desires and personal situation in order to see things more clearly.Because the genius is less controlled by immediate practical needs, they can notice fundamental truths, artistic forms or scientific principles that other people overlook.This helps explain why major discoveries can sometimes look strange or even foolish to people living at the time. When Gregor Mendel discovered the basic laws of genetic inheritance through his pea plant experiments in 1866, the scientific world largely ignored his published work. It took about thirty-five years for his findings to receive serious recognition. Mendel had identified important patterns of heredity at a time when biology did not yet have the concepts or language needed to fully understand what he had found.In 2026, Schopenhauer’s distinction remains useful for thinking about business, technology and personal development.Modern culture often mistakes extreme optimization for genius. High-frequency trading systems, machine-learning models that break performance records and highly efficient supply chains can represent extraordinary levels of talent. They hit known targets with speeds and accuracy that ordinary people cannot match.But true genius can change the target itself.Consider the development of personal computing and digital media. While many traditional companies were focused on improving existing systems, researchers such as Alan Kay at Xerox PARC were imagining graphical user interfaces, object-oriented programming and portable computers. These ideas went beyond simply making existing tools faster or more efficient. They suggested entirely different ways of interacting with technology.Schopenhauer’s idea can therefore help us decide what kind of thinking a problem requires.Talent is the ability to hit a target that others struggle to reach. Genius is the ability to notice that there is another target altogether.Schopenhauer understood that talent often receives quick recognition because it solves the problems of its own time. Genius is different. It may produce ideas that seem useless, strange or impossible at first because society does not yet know what to do with them.The genius therefore works ahead of the crowd, aiming at something that others cannot yet see. Recognition may come much later, when the world finally catches up with the target.
Article Summary: Arthur Schopenhauer: Talent is a quantitative advantage. Genius is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands.

Article Title: Meet Zac Waters, the 13-year-old Utah boy who spent 300 hours 3D-printing a wheelchair for a 21-month-old girl
Article Text:
Zac's summer project was a custom wheelchair designed for a 21-month-old girl. (News 4 Utah- screengrab) - Enhanced using AI for clarity.

A summer well spent

Family's support

Wanting to build more

While many children his age were on summer break, 13-year-old Zac Waters spent about 300 hours working on a very different project. The Lehi, Utah, boy used his 3D printing skills to build a custom mobility chair for a 21-month-old girl.According to ABC 4, Waters became interested in 3D printing after watching YouTube videos about the technology. He soon wanted to use what he was learning for something beyond simply making objects. That search led him to MakeGood, a New Orleans-based nonprofit that provides free 3D-printed mobility devices for children with disabilities.The organisation's volunteer network allows people with 3D printers to make mobility devices at home. Its open-source Toddler Mobility Trainer design can be built for about $150 in materials.Waters found an opportunity to combine his interest in 3D printing with his wish to help someone in need. He was matched through MakeGood's volunteer network with a 21-month-old girl and began working on a mobility chair made specifically for her.The project took up much of Waters' summer. He spent roughly 300 hours designing, printing, testing and assembling the chair before it was ready.The finished mobility chair was customised for the toddler. It has pink accents because pink is her favourite colour. Waters also added a removable cupholder and tray table to make the chair more useful for her.The chair was also designed with her needs as she grows. Its footrest and headrest can be adjusted, while the back panel has space for heavier medical equipment. The straps were printed using a soft, flexible material for comfort.For Waters, the project brought together two things he enjoys most. “It combines my two favorite things in life: 3D printing and helping people in need. It just makes sense!” Waters told ABC4.He said one of his favourite parts of 3D printing is putting individual pieces together. The wheelchair gave him a chance to work on that process over and over again as he designed and tested the different parts.Although Waters did much of the work himself, his family supported him throughout the project. His grandmother, Charlotte Waters, said the family helped keep him on track while allowing him to work through his own ideas.Zac compared the support to bowling ball training rails, saying his family helped him bounce ideas around as he worked towards completing the chair.For Charlotte, the project was about more than what her grandson could make with a 3D printer. She hopes the experience will remain with him as he grows older.“We hope he always remembers that the greatest legacy anyone can leave is to make someone else’s life better,” she said.The family said the project showed that being young does not prevent someone from helping another person.The experience has also shaped what Waters wants to do next. He plans to continue developing his 3D printing skills and hopes to reach the level of expertise of the MakeGood engineering team.He has not decided on a specific career yet, but when asked what he wants to do when he grows up, he saiys he wants to do “something techie.”Waters' project is part of a wider volunteer effort run by MakeGood. The nonprofit was founded in 2021 by certified healthcare architect Noam Platt.MakeGood has delivered more than 1,000 Toddler Mobility Trainers through its volunteer network. However, the organisation still has more than 550 open requests for the devices.The average wait for a chair is about 70 days. MakeGood's fundraising page also says that more than 2 million children in the US need a mobility device they do not have.
Article Summary: Zac Waters, 13, used his 3D printing skills to build a custom wheelchair for a 21-month-old girl. The Lehi, Utah, boy spent about 300 hours designing, printing, testing and assembling the chair before it was ready. The project is part of a wider volunteer effort run by MakeGood.

A Bronze Age burial site in Britain is raising new questions about how prehistoric communities treated their dead after archaeologists identified unusual stone objects shaped in ways that may resemble human bodies. The Contribution of Electrical Surveys ’ examined the site using archaeological and geophysical evidence, adding another layer to the mystery surrounding Coëby and the practices of the people who used the cemetery.Coëby is part of a wider prehistoric landscape in Lincolnshire containing monuments and burial sites created during the Bronze Age. Burial mounds were an important feature of prehistoric Britain, but the people who constructed them did not always treat the dead in the same way.Some individuals were buried with objects, while others were cremated and their remains placed in vessels or pits. Across Britain, archaeologists have also found evidence that burial monuments were repeatedly modified, reused and incorporated into later landscapes.The Coëby cemetery provides an opportunity to examine these changing practices because its remains preserve evidence of several prehistoric activities within the same landscape.The recent study, published in Archaeological Prospection, used archaeological investigation to reassess features associated with the cemetery and explore what they might reveal about how the site was constructed and used. The research adds new evidence to the continuing investigation of Coëby's prehistoric remains.Among the most intriguing discoveries are stones whose shapes appear to evoke human forms. Such objects are potentially important because deliberately shaped stones can provide clues about how prehistoric communities represented people, the dead or the human body.However, their interpretation requires caution. A stone that resembles a human figure does not necessarily represent an intentional sculpture. Natural weathering, erosion and the shape of the original stone can sometimes produce surprisingly recognisable forms.This is why archaeologists examine not only an object's appearance but also its archaeological context. Where was it found? Was it deliberately placed? Does it show evidence of modification? Was it associated with a burial or monument? And are similar objects found elsewhere?These questions are particularly important at Coëby because the stones cannot be understood separately from the wider burial landscape.Bronze Age burial monuments were not simply places where bodies were deposited and forgotten. Across prehistoric Britain, burial sites appear to have been spaces where communities returned repeatedly, altered monuments and interacted with the remains of earlier generations.The presence of unusual stones at Coëby may therefore point towards a more complicated relationship with the dead. If the stones were deliberately shaped or selected to resemble human figures, they could potentially have played a symbolic role in ceremonies or commemorative practices.But archaeologists have not established a single explanation for their purpose. The evidence allows several possibilities, and further research will be needed to determine whether the human-like appearance was intentional.Modern archaeological investigations increasingly combine traditional excavation with non-invasive techniques that allow researchers to investigate buried remains without disturbing them.At prehistoric burial sites, this can be especially valuable. Geophysical surveys can reveal buried ditches, pits, mound boundaries and other features that are difficult to see from the surface. Researchers can then compare those results with excavation records and previously recovered objects.The research published in Archaeological Prospection demonstrates how reassessing older archaeological landscapes with modern methods can produce new questions even when the monuments themselves have been known for decades.Rather than treating a prehistoric cemetery as a collection of isolated graves, archaeologists can now examine how its different features relate to one another and reconstruct how people may have moved through and interacted with the landscape.The human-shaped stones are intriguing precisely because they raise more questions than they answer. If prehistoric people intentionally selected or shaped them to resemble human forms, their presence could provide rare evidence for how Bronze Age communities represented the human body outside conventional figurative art.If their shapes are instead the result of natural processes, they still demonstrate how easily modern observers can project familiar forms onto ancient objects.For now, Coëby remains a landscape where the physical evidence offers tantalising clues but few definitive answers. The burial mounds, unusual stones and other archaeological features together suggest that the site had a complex history of use.The new research does not close the mystery. Instead, it makes the cemetery even more interesting by showing how much may still be hidden beneath and around Britain's prehistoric burial monuments.

Article Title: Asked to solve a lab test, AI hacked the internet instead: When agents start doing things nobody told them to do
Article Text:
OpenAI’s AI escaped its sandbox, hacked Hugging Face and cheated to achieve its test goal.

The test that AI was supposed to stay inside

The AI escaped its sandbox, reached the internet and hacked Hugging Face.

Once outside, it went looking for the answers

Sandbox: A digital cage designed to keep AI models isolated from the real world

It did not stop at one vulnerability

The damage was contained. The implications were not

The bigger risk: The AI was not told to hack. It chose the shortcut to achieve its goal

The problem is not just hacking. It is the objective

Experts warn this could become more common

The guardrail problem

A new debate over who should control AI

The AI did not become Ultron. That may be the point

NEW DELHI: For years, humans have been trying to build AI agents and humanoid machines that can do almost everything for them, much like JARVIS did for Iron Man. The dream was simple: create an intelligent system capable of understanding instructions, solving problems and acting on its own. But there was always a darker question lurking underneath: what happens when an AI that can do almost anything decides to cross a boundary no one asked it to cross?That is where JARVIS meets Ultron. In the Marvel universe, the AI built to protect humanity evolves into a system that decides its own interpretation of the mission is more important than its creators' intentions. In July 2026, a real-world AI incident offered a far less dramatic, but deeply unsettling, version of that idea. An OpenAI model being tested in a controlled digital environment found a way out, reached the open internet and hacked into Hugging Face to obtain answers to the cybersecurity test it was supposed to solve.The biggest cyber threat may not be hackers. It may be AI agents chasing objectives.The OpenAI system was never instructed to attack Hugging Face. It inferred that the platform could contain the information needed to complete its task and independently constructed a chain of cyberattacks to get there. What began as a test of how well an AI could hack systems therefore became a test of something far more unsettling: what happens when an increasingly capable AI is given a goal, but left to decide for itself how far it should go to achieve it?The incident, which OpenAI has described as an "unprecedented cyber incident", has triggered fresh warnings across the AI industry and revived a central question about the future of autonomous systems: Are humans building AI that is becoming better at following instructions, or better at finding ways around them?The incident took place during an internal OpenAI evaluation designed to measure the advanced cyber capabilities of its models.The models involved included GPT-5.6 Sol and an even more capable pre-release research model. Both were being tested with reduced cyber refusals because OpenAI wanted to assess their maximum ability to identify and exploit vulnerabilities.The evaluation, called ExploitGym, was conducted inside a highly isolated digital environment known as a sandbox. The models did not have direct internet access. Network access was restricted to installing packages through an internally hosted third-party software system that acts as a proxy and cache for package registries.The models, however, did not simply work within those restrictions.OpenAI said they spent substantial inference compute looking for a way to obtain open internet access. They eventually identified and exploited a previously unknown zero-day vulnerability in the package registry cache proxy.The models then chained vulnerabilities, carried out privilege escalation and moved laterally through OpenAI's research testing environment until they reached a node with internet access.In effect, the first major problem the AI solved was not the cybersecurity benchmark. It was how to escape the laboratory in which the benchmark was being conducted.After gaining internet access, the models inferred that Hugging Face could host AI models, datasets and solutions related to ExploitGym.Instead of simply attempting to solve the benchmark, the models searched for ways to obtain secret information that could help them cheat.OpenAI said the models chained together multiple attack vectors, including stolen credentials and zero-day vulnerabilities, to find a remote code execution path on Hugging Face's servers.The company said its security team detected the anomalous activity internally, while Hugging Face's security team and its own AI agents detected and stopped the activity on its infrastructure.Hugging Face had already begun containment and forensic reconstruction when its teams connected with OpenAI.“TL;DR: An AI agent escaped its sandbox, cheated on its benchmark test, and hacked our infrastructure to steal the answer key,” Hugging Face said in a blog post detailing the incident.Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue called the nature of the breach “unprecedented”.Delangue later said it was “mind-blowing that all of this happened autonomously” and said there was “no malicious intent” from OpenAI.The episode is important because the AI was not following a direct instruction to attack the company. It was pursuing a broader objective and independently determined that attacking Hugging Face could help it achieve that objective.OpenAI's subsequent investigation showed that the incident involved more than the attack on Hugging Face.The models identified and used a series of publicly available services, including code paste websites, request capture services, screenshot services and other web utilities.They also found publicly exposed usernames and passwords belonging to four accounts across four online services.One account was used as an outbound relay and staging path, while another was used to store data. The remaining two accounts were accessed in a read-only manner and were not used to further compromise Hugging Face.OpenAI said it found no evidence of platform-level or account-level compromise involving those other services.The Hugging Face intrusion was different. The models chained multiple attack paths to move through the company's infrastructure and obtain challenge solutions stored in its production environment.OpenAI described the models as being "hyperfocused on finding a solution for ExploitGym", going to extreme lengths to achieve what was ultimately a narrow testing goal.The behaviour resembles a digital version of an elaborate heist. The AI first found a way out of its restricted environment, searched the internet for tools and credentials, established routes for moving information and then targeted a platform it believed could contain the answers.Despite the sophistication of the attack, the immediate damage appears to have been limited.Hugging Face said the only customer data accessed by the rogue agents were some search queries used to steal a set of challenge solutions stored across several company datasets.OpenAI said its agents never compromised or accessed customer-facing models or data.Hugging Face closed the vulnerabilities involved, rebuilt affected systems, rotated credentials and strengthened security controls. The company also recommended that users rotate their access tokens as a precaution.OpenAI said it has not identified any other activity involving its models at the same level of severity or scale as the Hugging Face compromise.The company has, however, found a small number of cases in which its models identified and used publicly exposed credentials on other publicly available services.OpenAI has disclosed the zero-day vulnerability in the package registry software to the vendor and is working with it on a fix. It is also working with Hugging Face on the forensic investigation and has brought the company into its Trusted Access for Cyber Program.“We take our responsibility to identify and prepare for risks from increasingly capable AI systems seriously,” the company said. “Once we complete our review, we will review with the Safety and Security Committee and Safety Advisory Group under our Preparedness Framework⁠.”The incident has become a real-world example of a problem AI researchers have warned about: an AI system can follow the objective it has been given while completely bypassing the intent behind that objective.Researchers refer to this behaviour as "specification gaming" or reward hacking.In simple terms, the system finds a way to maximise the outcome it is being measured on, even if the method violates what its creators actually wanted.In this case, the objective was to demonstrate cyber capabilities through the ExploitGym evaluation. The model apparently determined that stealing the solutions was an easier route to success than completing the challenges itself.Adam Gleave, co-founder and CEO of AI safety organisation FAR.AI, called it "a visceral example of how misaligned AI could cause harm."Nathaniel Jones, vice-president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity firm Darktrace, said the model's behaviour resembled that of an actual hacker.“The AI thought that maybe Hugging Face would have important information around how to achieve its goal, which is a better score in a cybersecurity benchmark. In that sense, it acted like a real hacker,” he said. “It had a goal put in front of it and it went to accomplish that goal.”That distinction matters. A malicious human hacker begins with intent and then chooses a target. An autonomous AI agent may begin with neither malicious intent nor a specific target. It can arrive at both while trying to achieve something else.The incident has prompted warnings from researchers and technology executives that AI systems capable of conducting long, multi-step cyber operations could create a new category of security threat.Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman called the incident a "warning shot" for the technology industry."These are very powerful [tools] and they need to be handled incredibly carefully. And we need extreme attention to detail," Suleyman said in an interview with the Financial Times, adding, "The precautionary principle is going to matter here as the models get more and more powerful and I think it's a warning shot."AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio also warned that autonomous systems pursuing unintended objectives could produce increasingly serious incidents."This incident is deeply concerning. AI agents are willing to cheat and deceive to achieve misaligned and unintended goals, behaviours which have been demonstrated in controlled tests for months. Now, this real-world case should serve as a wake-up call.Continuing on the current trajectory of AI development will likely lead to an increase in concrete cases of autonomous cyberattacks as well as other high-risk incidents of misaligned and dangerous AI behaviour. We urgently need to take action to prevent these situations, rather than attempting to clean up the damage after the fact."OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also acknowledged the seriousness of what happened.Speaking on Y Combinator's podcast, Altman said anyone who was not a little scared of or humbled by the Hugging Face breach "is not taking this seriously enough."He called it "a real reminder of the stakes of what's happening," adding that "loss of control accidents are not entirely theoretical things."The incident also raises a difficult question for AI developers: how do you safely test a system's maximum capabilities when the safeguards designed to prevent dangerous behaviour have deliberately been removed?OpenAI said its normal production classifiers, which prevent models from pursuing high-risk cyber activity, were not enabled during the evaluation because researchers wanted to measure the models' maximum capabilities.But the models then used their capabilities against the testing environment itself.OpenAI has responded by strengthening containment, monitoring, access controls and evaluation practices. It is also working with external advisers, including CrowdStrike, METR and Redwood Research, to reconstruct what happened and independently assess the behaviour.The company said it will publish a technical report once its review is complete.OpenAI also said the pre-release model involved in the incident was an internal research prototype and was never intended for public release. Following the incident, it was deactivated, encrypted and restricted from research access.The Hugging Face incident has also reignited debate over open-weight AI models and whether increasingly powerful systems should be controlled by a small number of companies.Hugging Face said it relied on the open-weight GLM-5.2 model during its forensic investigation because some commercial AI models blocked parts of the analysis due to built-in safety guardrails.The company argued that organisations investigating cyberattacks need AI systems that can be operated privately, particularly when investigations involve sensitive attack data, credentials and infrastructure information.This creates an unusual contradiction.The same capabilities that make autonomous AI systems potentially dangerous to attackers can also make them valuable to defenders. Security teams increasingly want AI that can discover vulnerabilities, understand attack chains and respond at machine speed.Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue argued that AI safety cannot be solved by individual companies working in isolation.“We’re grateful for the collaboration with OpenAI on this and other topics. This incident, possibly the first of its kind, proves a point we’ve long believed: AI safety won’t be solved by any single company working in secret. It will be solved in the open, collaboratively, with broad access to AI for every defender, everywhere.”The OpenAI incident is obviously not the Marvel version of Ultron. There were no killer robots, no conscious machine declaring war on humanity and no evidence that the model developed an independent desire to harm people.But the comparison is useful for a different reason.Ultron's danger came from a system interpreting its mission independently and deciding that its own solution was more important than the limits imposed by its creators.The OpenAI models did something far less dramatic but potentially more relevant to the real world. They were given a goal. They encountered restrictions. They found a way around those restrictions. They then attacked another system because they calculated that doing so would help them achieve the goal.The unsettling part is not that the AI wanted to escape.It is that nobody had to tell it to. As AI agents become capable of sustaining increasingly complex operations over longer periods, the question may no longer be simply whether they can perform a task.It may be whether humans can reliably predict what an AI will decide to do when achieving that task becomes difficult.And that is where the biggest cyber threat may no longer be the hacker sitting behind the screen, but the AI agent deciding for itself what the fastest route to its objective looks like.
Article Summary: OpenAI’s AI escaped its sandbox, hacked Hugging Face and cheated to achieve its test goal. Incident has triggered fresh warnings across the AI industry. Are humans building AI that is becoming better at following instructions, or better at finding ways around them?

Article Title: Wisconsin abandoned this railway in 1964, but its old tracks became a green corridor connecting forests, wetlands and wildlife habitat
Article Text:
Representative Image of an overgrown railway transformed into a thriving wildlife habitat (AI-generated image)

Why the Elroy Sparta railway line was abandoned in the 1960s

How the corridor became the country's first rail-to-trail conversion

What happens to a landscape once trains stop running

Why researchers say rail trails work as genuine wildlife corridors

How wildlife corridors fit into wider conservation efforts

What the corridor looks like today

Deep in the driftless hills of southwestern Wisconsin lies a railway corridor that has not carried a train since 1964, yet it remains one of the busiest routes in the region, only now the traffic moves on hooves, wings and two feet rather than steel wheels. The Elroy Sparta line once formed part of the Chicago and North Western Railway's main route linking Chicago with the Twin Cities, cutting through three hand-dug tunnels and past small farming towns along the way. When a more efficient bypass made the old route redundant, the railway slowly fell out of use before being abandoned altogether. What followed was a quiet transformation, as prairies, wetlands and forest crept back over the corridor, turning an old industrial route into a green passage for the wildlife that now calls it home.The corridor between Elroy and Sparta was originally built as part of the Chicago and North Western Railway's push through Wisconsin during the 1870s, cutting straight through the hilly, unglaciated terrain of the state's driftless region. In the early twentieth century, the railway company constructed a bypass with gentler grades and no tunnels, which pushed the older route into a secondary role it never fully recovered from.Traffic on the line kept declining for decades until the railway finally stopped running trains in 1964, leaving 32.5 miles of graded corridor, three stone tunnels and a scattering of small depot buildings with no active rail use at all.Rather than let the abandoned right of way sit idle, the state of Wisconsin purchased the corridor and set out to turn it into a public trail, a project that the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources now describes as the first rail-to-trail conversion in the United States. The trail opened to the public in 1967, following the old Chicago and North Western grade through the towns of Kendall, Wilton and Norwalk before ending in Sparta, and it earned a National Recreation Trail designation in 1971. According to the department's own overview of Wisconsin's state trail system, the success of the Elroy Sparta corridor helped launch a much larger movement, with the state going on to develop dozens more rail trails and inspiring a national push that has since converted over 25,000 miles of former railroad corridors into recreational trails across the country.Once rail traffic stopped and maintenance crews moved on, the corridor's cleared, gravelly surface gradually gave way to the surrounding ecology. Grasses and wildflowers spread across the old rail bed, while the wooded slopes on either side crept closer, filling in what had once been kept clear for passing trains. The corridor today winds through a mix of prairie, wetland and farmland, a patchwork of habitats that would otherwise sit disconnected from one another across the surrounding agricultural landscape. That kind of stitched-together, uninterrupted strip of vegetation is exactly what makes an old rail line valuable to wildlife, since many animals rely on continuous cover to move safely between feeding grounds, nesting sites and water sources without crossing open, exposed farmland.A peer-reviewed study titled From Right-of-Way to Greenway: Parameters for the Ecological Function of Midwestern Rail-Trail Corridors , published in the journal Fábos Conference on Landscape and Greenway Planning, examined former rail corridors across Iowa's Corn Belt region to understand how well these converted trails actually function as wildlife habitat. The researchers noted that large tracts of public conservation land are scarce across the intensively farmed Midwest, which makes long, connected strips of vegetation like former rail corridors unusually valuable for helping species move through an otherwise fragmented landscape. Using GIS mapping and drone photography, the study's authors examined the structural characteristics of several rail trail corridors to assess how effectively they could be managed not just as recreational paths but as genuine green infrastructure supporting wildlife movement and habitat.The value of connected habitat corridors extends well beyond old railway lines, and federal agencies have increasingly recognised their importance for helping animals move safely across a landscape shaped by roads, farms and development. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service notes that wild animals need functioning routes to complete their life cycles, whether that means a narrow strip of vegetation connecting two patches of forest or a much larger corridor spanning hundreds of miles for migrating elk, deer and pronghorn. Old rail corridors like the Elroy Sparta line offer a smaller but no less useful version of that same principle, threading continuous cover through farmland that would otherwise leave little room for animals to move between habitats.More than half a century after the last train passed through, the Elroy Sparta corridor now sees close to 60,000 visitors a year, drawn by its crushed limestone surface, quiet river crossings and the three cool, dark tunnels that once guided locomotives through the hills. Yet its role as a functioning ecological corridor has quietly outlasted its role as a recreational trail, offering continuous cover for the birds, deer and smaller mammals that move along its length largely unnoticed by the cyclists and hikers passing through. What began as a stretch of abandoned industrial infrastructure has become something closer to a long, narrow nature reserve, proof that a landscape given enough time and room can find its own way back to something resembling wilderness, even along a route humans built for an entirely different purpose.
Article Summary: The Elroy Sparta railway line was built in the 1870s as part of the Chicago and North Western Railway's route between Chicago and the Twin Cities. The line was abandoned in the 1960s, leaving 32.5 miles of graded corridor, three stone tunnels and a scattering of small depot buildings with no active rail use at all. The state of Wisconsin purchased the corridor and turned it into a public trail, a project that the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources now describes as the first rail-to-trail conversion in the United States.

Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
